questions.title: PostgreSQL vs MySQL — Key Differences
questions.question: What are the key differences between PostgreSQL and MySQL, and why would you choose PostgreSQL for a Java backend?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- PostgreSQL: object-relational, true SQL standard compliance, stronger ACID guarantees
- MySQL: faster simple reads historically, simpler setup, wider shared hosting availability
- PostgreSQL advantages: advanced data types (JSONB, arrays, ranges, enums), window functions, CTEs, full-text search, PostGIS
- PostgreSQL MVCC: readers never block writers; MySQL InnoDB also has MVCC but behaves differently
- PostgreSQL uses serializable snapshot isolation; MySQL relies more on lock-based approaches
- For complex queries, analytics, and JSON workloads: PostgreSQL is generally superior

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
PostgreSQL is an object-relational database that strictly follows the SQL standard and has a much richer feature set. For a Java backend, it's generally the better choice because of its support for complex data types like JSONB for flexible schema columns, arrays, range types, and powerful features like window functions, recursive CTEs, and full-text search — all built in without plugins.

MySQL historically had faster simple read performance and is simpler to set up, which made it popular for web applications in the early 2000s. But for the kind of analytical and complex transactional queries a Java backend typically runs, PostgreSQL's query planner and execution engine are generally superior.

PostgreSQL's MVCC implementation means readers never block writers and writers never block readers. A long-running report query won't hold up inserts. This is crucial for a backend that needs to handle concurrent reads and writes without one type of operation starving the other.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Feature Comparison

| Feature | PostgreSQL | MySQL |
|---------|-----------|-------|
| SQL compliance | Excellent | Partial |
| JSONB support | Native, indexed | JSON type, limited |
| Window functions | Full support | Basic support |
| Full-text search | Built-in | Via MyISAM or plugin |
| Array types | Native | Not supported |
| Range types | Native | Not supported |
| Partitioning | Declarative (PG10+) | Available |
| Materialized views | Supported | Not natively |
| Custom types/functions | Extensive | Limited |

## Spring Boot Configuration

```yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/appdb
    driver-class-name: org.postgresql.Driver
  jpa:
    database-platform: org.hibernate.dialect.PostgreSQLDialect
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate  # use Flyway/Liquibase for migrations
```

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
    <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>
```

questions.title: PostgreSQL Data Types for Java Backends
questions.question: What are the most useful PostgreSQL data types for a Java backend that you should know?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- BIGINT for IDs (auto-increment with SERIAL/BIGSERIAL or IDENTITY)
- NUMERIC/DECIMAL for money — never use FLOAT for currency
- TIMESTAMPTZ stores time with timezone reference (use this over TIMESTAMP)
- VARCHAR vs TEXT: in PostgreSQL TEXT is not slower, length-constrained VARCHAR only matters for validation
- UUID: natively supported, good for distributed IDs
- JSONB: binary JSON with indexing support — vs JSON which just validates and stores text
- ENUM types: more readable than string, enforced by DB but costly to ALTER
- Arrays: store multiple values without a join table

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The data type choices that matter most in practice are around time, money, and flexible schema. For timestamps, always use TIMESTAMPTZ — timestamp with time zone — not plain TIMESTAMP. TIMESTAMPTZ stores everything in UTC and converts to the session timezone on display, which avoids an entire class of timezone bugs in distributed systems.

For monetary values, use NUMERIC or DECIMAL with explicit precision and scale — never a floating point type. Floats cannot represent many decimal values exactly, which leads to rounding errors in financial calculations. NUMERIC is exact.

JSONB is one of PostgreSQL's killer features. Unlike JSON which just validates and stores text as-is, JSONB parses the JSON into a binary format, stores it efficiently, and supports GIN indexing so you can query inside JSON documents with indexes. This gives you flexible schema storage without giving up the ability to search efficiently.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Essential Data Types

```sql
CREATE TABLE products (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,           -- auto-increment 64-bit int
    public_id   UUID DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),  -- URL-safe public identifier
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,                   -- no length limit, same perf as VARCHAR
    sku         VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE,              -- VARCHAR when you want DB-level length validation
    price       NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,         -- exact decimal — always for money
    stock       INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    tags        TEXT[],                          -- array of strings
    metadata    JSONB,                           -- binary JSON with index support
    status      product_status NOT NULL,         -- enum type
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),       -- with timezone: stores UTC, shows local
    updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Create enum type first
CREATE TYPE product_status AS ENUM ('draft', 'active', 'discontinued');
```

## TIMESTAMPTZ vs TIMESTAMP

```sql
-- TIMESTAMP: stores exactly what you give it — timezone agnostic (dangerous)
INSERT INTO events (ts) VALUES ('2024-01-01 10:00:00');  -- which timezone? unknown!

-- TIMESTAMPTZ: normalizes to UTC, renders in session timezone
SET timezone = 'America/New_York';
INSERT INTO events (tstz) VALUES (NOW());  -- stored as UTC
SELECT tstz FROM events;  -- displayed in New York time

SET timezone = 'Asia/Kolkata';
SELECT tstz FROM events;  -- same moment, displayed in IST
```

## Array Type — Avoid a Join Table

```sql
-- Tags without a join table
INSERT INTO articles (title, tags)
VALUES ('Java Tips', ARRAY['java', 'backend', 'jpa']);

-- Query articles with any of these tags
SELECT title FROM articles
WHERE tags && ARRAY['java', 'spring'];  -- && = overlap (any match)

-- Query articles with ALL these tags
WHERE tags @> ARRAY['java', 'backend'];  -- @> = contains all

-- Index for fast array queries
CREATE INDEX idx_article_tags ON articles USING GIN (tags);
```

## Java Type Mappings

| PostgreSQL | Java |
|------------|------|
| BIGINT | Long |
| NUMERIC | BigDecimal |
| BOOLEAN | Boolean |
| TEXT/VARCHAR | String |
| TIMESTAMPTZ | OffsetDateTime / Instant |
| UUID | java.util.UUID |
| JSONB | String / custom type |
| TEXT[] | String[] |

speakable_v2.cap: This gives you flexible schema storage without giving up the ability to search efficiently.

questions.title: MVCC — How PostgreSQL Handles Concurrency
questions.question: How does PostgreSQL's MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) work?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- MVCC: each transaction sees a snapshot of the DB at a point in time
- No read-write locking — readers don't block writers and vice versa
- How: each row version has xmin (created by tx) and xmax (deleted/updated by tx)
- A transaction only sees rows where xmin is committed and < its snapshot txid, and xmax is null or > its snapshot
- Dead tuples: old versions left behind after updates — VACUUM reclaims them
- Transaction ID wraparound: 32-bit txid, must VACUUM regularly to avoid wraparound catastrophe

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
MVCC works by keeping multiple versions of each row rather than locking rows for access. When you update a row, PostgreSQL doesn't overwrite the old data — it creates a new version of the row and marks the old version as deleted. Any transaction that started before your update still sees the old version. Any transaction that started after your update sees the new version.

This is what allows readers and writers to work concurrently without blocking each other. A long-running report query takes a snapshot at its start time and consistently sees that snapshot throughout its execution, even as other transactions are inserting and updating data in the same tables.

The cost of this approach is dead tuples — old row versions that are no longer visible to any active transaction. These accumulate continuously on a busy table and must be cleaned up by AUTOVACUUM. If AUTOVACUUM falls behind, tables and indexes bloat and performance degrades. This is why monitoring AUTOVACUUM behavior is an important PostgreSQL operational concern.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Row Versioning (Hidden Columns)

```sql
-- PostgreSQL stores hidden system columns per row
SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, name, salary FROM employees WHERE id = 1;
-- ctid:  physical location (page, offset)
-- xmin:  transaction that created this row version
-- xmax:  transaction that deleted/updated this row (0 = current)

-- After UPDATE:
-- Old row: xmin=100, xmax=205 (marked dead by tx 205)
-- New row: xmin=205, xmax=0  (current version)
```

## Snapshot Visibility

```
Transaction A starts (snapshot: sees txids < 200)
Transaction B starts (snapshot: sees txids < 200)

Transaction C (txid=201) updates row 1 and commits

Transaction A: still sees old row 1 (201 > A's snapshot boundary)
Transaction B: still sees old row 1 (same snapshot boundary)

Transaction D starts (snapshot: sees txids < 205)
Transaction D: sees new row 1 (201 < 205, and txid 201 is committed)
```

## VACUUM and Dead Tuple Cleanup

```sql
-- Monitor dead tuple accumulation
SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,
       last_autovacuum, last_analyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE n_dead_tup > 10000
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;

-- Manual vacuum when needed
VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) orders;

-- Full vacuum — reclaims disk space (requires exclusive lock, use during maintenance)
VACUUM FULL orders;
```

## Transaction ID Wraparound Prevention

```sql
-- 32-bit txid: ~2 billion values before wraparound
-- If transactions wrap, old data becomes invisible → database protection shutdown

-- Monitor oldest transactions still in use
SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) AS txid_age
FROM pg_database
ORDER BY txid_age DESC;
-- Alert if age > 1.5 billion — VACUUM FREEZE needed

-- Emergency freeze to prevent wraparound
VACUUM FREEZE table_name;
```

speakable_v2.hook: MVCC works by keeping multiple versions of each row rather than locking rows for access.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This is why monitoring AUTOVACUUM behavior is an important PostgreSQL operational concern.

questions.title: Full-Text Search in PostgreSQL
questions.question: How does full-text search work in PostgreSQL and how do you implement it in a Java Spring application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- tsvector: document converted to searchable token list with positions
- tsquery: search query with operators: & (AND), | (OR), ! (NOT), <-> (phrase)
- GIN index on tsvector column for fast full-text search
- ts_rank() for relevance scoring and ordering results by relevance
- to_tsvector(language, text) and to_tsquery(language, query)
- Stored generated column for tsvector to avoid recomputing on every search
- Alternative: Elasticsearch for very large-scale or advanced search needs

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
PostgreSQL has built-in full-text search that's good enough for many applications without needing an external search engine. It works by converting text into a tsvector — a list of lexemes, which are normalized word stems with their positions in the document. Searching converts the query into a tsquery and matches it against the tsvector.

The practical advantage over LIKE queries is that tsvector handles stemming — searching for 'run' also finds 'running' and 'runs'. It handles stop words like 'the' and 'a' which would produce too many results to be useful. And with a GIN index, full-text search is much faster than a LIKE '%keyword%' query which requires a full table scan.

For a Spring application, the typical setup is to add a generated tsvector column to your table that automatically updates whenever the source text columns change, index it with GIN, and query it using native SQL since JPA doesn't have first-class full-text support.

questions.title: PostgreSQL Schemas, Roles and Security
questions.question: How do PostgreSQL schemas and roles work, and how do you set up proper security for a Java application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Schema: namespace within a database — like a folder for tables
- Default schema: 'public' — best practice: create app-specific schema
- Role: user or group in PostgreSQL — roles can own objects and have granted privileges
- Principle of least privilege: app role should only have SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on needed tables, not DDL
- GRANT/REVOKE: control access at table, schema, or database level
- Row-level security (RLS): filter rows based on who's querying — multi-tenant enforcement
- search_path: controls which schema PostgreSQL looks in first

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A schema in PostgreSQL is a namespace — a logical grouping of tables, views, and functions within a database. You can have multiple schemas in one database, which is useful for organizing objects or for multi-tenant setups where each tenant has their own schema.

Roles are PostgreSQL's unified concept for users and groups. You create a role, grant it specific privileges, and your application connects as that role. The key principle is least privilege — your application role should only have the permissions it actually needs: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on specific tables. It should not have CREATE TABLE or DROP permissions, which prevents a SQL injection attack from being able to modify the schema.

Row-level security is a powerful feature for multi-tenant applications. You attach a policy to a table that filters which rows each role can see. The application sets a session variable for the current tenant ID, and the policy automatically restricts all queries to that tenant's rows without any application-level filtering code.

questions.title: JSONB — Flexible Schema in PostgreSQL
questions.question: How do you use JSONB in PostgreSQL for flexible schema storage and how do you query and index it?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- JSONB: binary JSON — parsed, de-duplicated keys, reordered — supports indexing
- JSON: plain text storage — preserves whitespace and key order — no indexing
- Operators: -> returns JSON, ->> returns text; #> and #>> for nested paths
- GIN index: index all keys in JSONB — fast for @> (containment) queries
- Expression index: index a specific JSONB key — faster for known key queries
- jsonb_set() to update specific keys without replacing entire object
- Pattern: use structured columns for queried fields, JSONB for flexible/optional metadata

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
JSONB is PostgreSQL's binary JSON column type. Unlike the JSON type which just validates and stores text as-is, JSONB parses the JSON into an internal binary format, removes duplicate keys, and normalizes whitespace. The benefit is that JSONB supports GIN indexing — you can create an index that covers all keys in the JSON document, enabling fast containment queries.

The choice between JSONB and structured columns is a design decision. A good rule of thumb: if you always need to query or filter on a field, make it a real column with an index. If it's variable metadata that you store and retrieve but don't typically filter by, JSONB is a good fit — it avoids schema migrations every time you add a new metadata field.

Updating specific keys in JSONB without replacing the entire document uses the jsonb_set function. This is important for efficiency and to avoid race conditions — replacing the entire JSON object in an UPDATE would lose concurrent changes to other keys in the same document.

questions.title: Database Migrations with Flyway
questions.question: How do you manage PostgreSQL schema migrations with Flyway in a Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Flyway: versioned SQL migration files applied in order, tracked in flyway_schema_history table
- Naming convention: V{version}__{description}.sql (two underscores)
- Never modify applied migrations — Flyway checksums prevent this from silently succeeding
- Repeatable migrations (R__): re-applied whenever their checksum changes (views, functions)
- Baseline: for existing databases, establish a baseline so Flyway knows where to start
- Rollback: Flyway OSS doesn't support SQL rollback scripts — design migrations as forward-only
- Spring Boot auto-runs migrations on startup before JPA initialization

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Flyway is a database migration tool that tracks which SQL scripts have been applied to your database using a history table. You write versioned SQL files that Flyway applies in version order. On application startup, Flyway checks which versions have already been applied and runs only the new ones. This makes deployments repeatable and auditable.

The golden rule with Flyway is to never modify a migration that has already been applied to any environment. Flyway stores a checksum for each migration and will refuse to start if a checksum doesn't match, protecting you from silently corrupting a database that already applied a different version of a script.

For production deployments, write migrations that are safe to run while the application is up — avoid long-running DDL that locks tables. Adding a new column is fast. Adding a NOT NULL column to a large table without a default requires a table rewrite, which can take minutes and block all writes. The safe pattern is to add the column as nullable first, backfill existing rows, then add the constraint separately.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Project Setup

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
    <artifactId>flyway-core</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
    <artifactId>flyway-database-postgresql</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  flyway:
    enabled: true
    locations: classpath:db/migration
    baseline-on-migrate: false  # true only for existing databases
```

## Migration File Examples

```
src/main/resources/db/migration/
├── V001__create_users_table.sql
├── V002__create_products_table.sql
├── V003__add_search_vector_to_products.sql
├── V004__create_orders_tables.sql
└── R__views_and_functions.sql  (repeatable — updates every time file changes)
```

```sql
-- V001__create_users_table.sql
CREATE TABLE app.users (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    email       VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON app.users (email);
```

```sql
-- V003__add_search_vector_to_products.sql
-- Safe zero-downtime migration: add nullable column, then add constraint
ALTER TABLE app.products
    ADD COLUMN search_vector TSVECTOR
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
        to_tsvector('english', coalesce(name, ''))
    ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX idx_products_fts ON app.products USING GIN (search_vector);
-- CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY won't work in a transaction;
-- use a separate repeatable script or manual step
```

## Zero-Downtime: Add NOT NULL Column Safely

```sql
-- V005__add_status_to_orders.sql
-- Step 1: Add nullable with default (fast)
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'pending';

-- Step 2: Backfill existing rows (run in small batches if table is huge)
UPDATE orders SET status = 'completed'
WHERE status IS NULL AND total_amount IS NOT NULL;

-- Step 3: Add NOT NULL constraint (fast if all rows filled)
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET NOT NULL;
```

questions.title: PostgreSQL Performance Monitoring
questions.question: What are the key PostgreSQL system views and tools you use to monitor and troubleshoot performance?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- pg_stat_activity: currently running queries, wait events, connection states
- pg_stat_user_tables: seq scans vs index scans, dead tuples, autovacuum timing
- pg_stat_user_indexes: which indexes are used (scans count)
- pg_stat_statements: aggregate query performance (total time, calls, mean, stddev)
- pg_locks: active locks and waiting queries
- EXPLAIN ANALYZE: query execution plan with actual stats
- log_min_duration_statement: capture slow queries in PostgreSQL logs

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
PostgreSQL exposes rich monitoring data through system views. The ones I check most often are pg_stat_activity for live query monitoring, pg_stat_statements for aggregate query performance analysis, and pg_stat_user_tables for understanding table health — particularly dead tuple accumulation and whether autovacuum is keeping up.

pg_stat_user_indexes is valuable for finding unused indexes. Any index that has zero or near-zero scans since the server last restarted is wasted overhead — it's slowing down writes without helping any queries. Dropping unused indexes is often an easy win for write-heavy tables.

For active incidents, pg_stat_activity combined with pg_locks lets you see which queries are waiting for locks and which queries are holding them. This is the first tool to reach for when the application suddenly slows and you suspect lock contention rather than a missing index.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Live Query Monitor

```sql
-- All active queries with duration
SELECT pid, usename, state,
       ROUND(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (NOW() - query_start))::NUMERIC, 1) AS seconds,
       wait_event_type, wait_event,
       LEFT(query, 100) AS query_preview
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state != 'idle'
  AND query NOT LIKE '%pg_stat_activity%'
ORDER BY seconds DESC NULLS LAST;
```

## Table Health Dashboard

```sql
SELECT relname,
       seq_scan,
       idx_scan,
       ROUND(100.0 * seq_scan / NULLIF(seq_scan + idx_scan, 0), 1) AS seq_pct,
       n_live_tup,
       n_dead_tup,
       ROUND(100.0 * n_dead_tup / NULLIF(n_live_tup + n_dead_tup, 0), 1) AS dead_pct,
       last_autovacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;

-- Alert: seq_pct > 50% on large tables = missing index
-- Alert: dead_pct > 10% = autovacuum not keeping up
```

## Top Slow Queries (pg_stat_statements)

```sql
SELECT LEFT(query, 80) AS query,
       calls,
       total_exec_time::INT AS total_ms,
       mean_exec_time::INT  AS avg_ms,
       stddev_exec_time::INT AS stddev_ms
FROM pg_stat_statements
WHERE calls > 10
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 15;
```

## Lock Contention Check

```sql
SELECT
    blocked.pid         AS waiting_pid,
    blocked.query       AS waiting_query,
    blocking.pid        AS blocking_pid,
    blocking.query      AS blocking_query,
    NOW() - blocked.query_start AS waiting_duration
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking
    ON blocking.pid = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid))
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid)) > 0;
```

speakable_v2.hook: PostgreSQL exposes rich monitoring data through system views.
speakable_v2.cap: This is the first tool to reach for when the application suddenly slows and you suspect lock contention rather than a missing index.

questions.title: JSONB Indexing and Advanced Queries
questions.question: How do you efficiently query and index deeply nested JSONB data in PostgreSQL?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- GIN with default ops: supports @> (containment) and ? (key exists) — covers most cases
- jsonb_path_ops GIN: smaller index, only @> — faster for containment queries
- Expression index: (metadata->>'brand') — fast equality on specific key
- jsonpath: SQL/JSON path language for complex traversal and filtering
- jsonb_each() / jsonb_array_elements(): expand JSONB to rows for complex aggregation
- Update strategies: jsonb_set() for specific keys, || for merging objects

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
For JSONB indexing, the choice of GIN operator class matters. The default GIN index supports both @> containment queries and ? key-existence queries but stores more data. Using jsonb_path_ops gives a smaller, faster index but only supports @> containment — no key-existence checks.

For frequently queried specific keys, an expression index on the extracted text value is faster than a full GIN index because it's a smaller, more targeted B-tree index. Something like an index on (metadata ->> 'brand') enables fast equality and range queries on that single key.

jsonpath is the modern way to write complex JSON traversal. It's a path language similar to XPath for XML that can filter arrays, navigate nested objects, and apply predicates in a single readable expression rather than chaining multiple operators.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## GIN Index Options

```sql
-- Default GIN: supports @>, ?, ?|, ?&
CREATE INDEX idx_meta_gin ON products USING GIN (metadata);

-- jsonb_path_ops: smaller, faster for @> only
CREATE INDEX idx_meta_path ON products USING GIN (metadata jsonb_path_ops);
-- Use when you only need containment queries

-- Expression index: for equality on a known key
CREATE INDEX idx_meta_brand ON products ((metadata ->> 'brand'));
-- Supports: WHERE metadata ->> 'brand' = 'TechCo' with B-tree efficiency
```

## Advanced Queries

```sql
-- Containment: products with both tags
WHERE metadata @> '{"tags": ["laptop", "pro"]}'::jsonb;

-- Key exists
WHERE metadata ? 'discount_code';

-- jsonpath: products with ram > 8
WHERE metadata @@ '$.specs.ram > 8';

-- jsonpath exists: has any item with price < 100 in array
WHERE jsonb_path_exists(metadata, '$.items[*] ? (@.price < 100)');

-- jsonpath query: extract matching items
SELECT jsonb_path_query_array(metadata, '$.items[*] ? (@.category == "electronics")')
FROM orders;
```

## Expand JSONB for Aggregation

```sql
-- Expand array of order items to rows
SELECT order_id,
       item ->> 'product_id' AS product_id,
       (item ->> 'quantity')::INT AS qty,
       (item ->> 'price')::NUMERIC AS price
FROM orders,
     jsonb_array_elements(metadata -> 'items') AS item;

-- Expand object keys to rows
SELECT product_id, key, value
FROM products,
     jsonb_each_text(metadata) AS kv(key, value)
WHERE key LIKE 'spec_%';
```

## Partial JSONB Updates in Spring

```java
@Modifying
@Query(value = """
    UPDATE products
    SET metadata = jsonb_set(metadata, '{stock}', :stock::jsonb)
    WHERE id = :id
    """, nativeQuery = true)
void updateStock(@Param("id") Long id, @Param("stock") String stock);

// Call: repo.updateStock(1L, "42");
```

questions.title: Advanced Window Functions in PostgreSQL
questions.question: What are the most powerful window function patterns in PostgreSQL for analytics and reporting?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- ROWS vs RANGE frame modes: ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE counts logical groups by value
- NTILE(n): divide result into n equal buckets
- PERCENT_RANK and CUME_DIST: relative position within window
- First/last value: FIRST_VALUE(), LAST_VALUE() within partition
- NAMED WINDOWS: define once, reuse in multiple window functions
- FILTER clause with window functions for conditional window aggregation
- Performance: window functions processed after WHERE/GROUP BY — use CTEs to pre-filter

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Window functions become really powerful when you understand frame clauses. The frame defines the exact set of rows each calculation uses relative to the current row. ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING gives you a running total from the beginning to the current row. ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW gives you a 7-day moving average. RANGE BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING gives you a reverse running total from the current row to the end.

NTILE is great for percentile bucketing — it divides your result into equal-sized buckets. So NTILE(100) gives you percentile ranks, which is how you find the top 10% of customers or the bottom quartile of products.

Named windows are a readability feature that matters when you have multiple window functions over the same partition. Instead of repeating PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC in every function call, you define the window once with a name and reference it multiple times.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Frame Clauses

```sql
SELECT date, revenue,
  -- Running total from start to current row
  SUM(revenue) OVER (
    ORDER BY date
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS cumulative,

  -- 7-day moving average (current + 6 preceding)
  AVG(revenue) OVER (
    ORDER BY date
    ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS moving_avg_7d,

  -- Revenue as % of total for that month
  revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER (
    PARTITION BY DATE_TRUNC('month', date)
  ) * 100 AS pct_of_month
FROM daily_revenue;
```

## NTILE Percentile Bucketing

```sql
-- Bucket customers into revenue quartiles
SELECT customer_id,
       total_revenue,
       NTILE(4)   OVER (ORDER BY total_revenue DESC) AS quartile,
       NTILE(100) OVER (ORDER BY total_revenue DESC) AS percentile
FROM customer_revenue;
-- quartile=1 → top 25%, quartile=4 → bottom 25%
```

## Named Windows

```sql
SELECT department, name, salary,
  AVG(salary)      OVER dept_window AS dept_avg,
  MAX(salary)      OVER dept_window AS dept_max,
  ROW_NUMBER()     OVER dept_window AS dept_rank,
  PERCENT_RANK()   OVER dept_window AS relative_rank
FROM employees
WINDOW dept_window AS (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC);
-- Define window once, reuse four times
```

## FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE

```sql
SELECT name, salary, department,
  FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (
    PARTITION BY department
    ORDER BY salary DESC
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  ) AS highest_earner,
  LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (
    PARTITION BY department
    ORDER BY salary DESC
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  ) AS lowest_earner
FROM employees;
-- IMPORTANT: LAST_VALUE requires explicit UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING or it defaults to current row
```

questions.title: PostgreSQL Configuration and Performance Tuning
questions.question: What are the key PostgreSQL configuration parameters you should tune for a Java backend application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- shared_buffers: DB cache (25% of RAM is starting point)
- effective_cache_size: tells planner how much OS cache is available (50-75% RAM)
- work_mem: per-sort/hash operation memory — affects query performance for complex queries
- maintenance_work_mem: for VACUUM, index builds — set higher during maintenance
- max_connections: limit and use a connection pooler (PgBouncer) instead of raising this
- wal_buffers: write-ahead log buffer size
- checkpoint_completion_target: spread checkpoint writes over time (0.9 recommended)
- random_page_cost: reduce for SSD (1.1 vs 4.0 default)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The most impactful configuration change for most PostgreSQL installations is shared_buffers. This is how much memory PostgreSQL dedicates to caching data pages. The default is only 128MB, which is very conservative. A good starting point is 25% of available RAM — so on a 32GB server, set it to 8GB.

work_mem is subtle but important. It controls how much memory each sort or hash operation can use before spilling to disk. The catch is that complex queries can spawn multiple sort operations, and each database connection can run multiple queries simultaneously. So if you set work_mem to 256MB and you have 100 connections each running a sort, that's 25GB potentially allocated. Set it low globally and raise it per-session for specific analytical queries.

For SSDs, lower random_page_cost from the default of 4.0 to something like 1.1. This setting tells the query planner the relative cost of random disk access versus sequential. The default assumes spinning disks where random access is 4x more expensive. For SSDs, random and sequential access times are nearly equal, so the planner should prefer index scans much more aggressively.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Key postgresql.conf Settings

```ini
# Memory (for a 32GB dedicated database server)
shared_buffers = 8GB               # 25% of RAM — primary DB cache
effective_cache_size = 24GB        # 75% RAM — hints to planner for index planning
work_mem = 32MB                    # per sort/hash op — multiply by connections × ops
maintenance_work_mem = 2GB         # for VACUUM, CREATE INDEX — higher is better

# WAL and Checkpoints
wal_buffers = 64MB                  # write-ahead log buffer
checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9  # spread checkpoint writes over 90% of interval
max_wal_size = 4GB                  # allow large WAL before checkpoint

# Connections
max_connections = 100               # keep low; use PgBouncer for the actual pool

# Query Planner
random_page_cost = 1.1             # SSD: near-equal to seq_page_cost (1.0)
effective_io_concurrency = 200     # SSD: number of concurrent I/O operations

# Logging
log_min_duration_statement = 1000  # log queries > 1 second
log_checkpoints = on
log_connections = on
log_lock_waits = on
```

## PgBouncer Connection Pooling

```ini
# pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
mydb = host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 dbname=mydb

[pgbouncer]
pool_mode = transaction    # best for stateless apps (releases connection after each tx)
max_client_conn = 1000     # clients (app servers) can connect up to this
default_pool_size = 20     # actual PostgreSQL connections per database+user pair
# Result: 1000 app connections → 20 actual PG connections
```

## work_mem — Per-Session Override

```java
// For a specific analytical query that needs more memory
@Query(value = """
    SET work_mem = '256MB';
    SELECT ...
    """, nativeQuery = true)
// Better: use a dedicated read replica for analytical queries
```

## Tune Autovacuum for High-Traffic Tables

```sql
-- Orders table gets millions of updates per day
ALTER TABLE orders SET (
    autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01,
    autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.005,
    autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 2  -- ms; 0 = no delay for urgent tables
);
```

questions.title: Advanced Table Partitioning Strategies
questions.question: What are the advanced partitioning strategies in PostgreSQL and when do you use each?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- RANGE: date/time series — most common, enables efficient archival
- LIST: by known category values (country, status, region)
- HASH: even distribution when no natural range or list
- Sub-partitioning: partition a partition (range by month, then hash within)
- Partition pruning: optimizer eliminates non-matching partitions — requires filter on partition key
- Global indexes: PostgreSQL 11+ supports unique constraints spanning all partitions
- pg_partman extension: automates creating and managing time-based partitions

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The three partitioning types serve different data distribution patterns. RANGE is for time-series or sequential data — events, orders, logs — where you frequently query a specific time window and want to archive old data by simply dropping old partitions. LIST is for data that belongs to known discrete categories — partitioning by country code, by tenant ID if you have a small fixed set of tenants, or by status. HASH is for when you have none of those patterns but the table is too large for one partition — you hash the primary key and distribute rows evenly.

Partition pruning is what makes partitioning valuable. If your WHERE clause includes a filter on the partition key, the planner skips all partitions that can't contain matching data. If your queries never filter on the partition key, you'll scan all partitions for every query and get no benefit — possibly worse performance due to partition overhead.

For time-based partitions, automate partition creation with the pg_partman extension or a scheduled job. Failing to create next month's partition before data arrives causes inserts to fail.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## LIST Partitioning

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
    id      BIGINT,
    email   TEXT,
    region  TEXT NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY LIST (region);

CREATE TABLE users_apac   PARTITION OF users FOR VALUES IN ('in', 'sg', 'jp', 'au');
CREATE TABLE users_emea   PARTITION OF users FOR VALUES IN ('uk', 'de', 'fr', 'ae');
CREATE TABLE users_amer   PARTITION OF users FOR VALUES IN ('us', 'ca', 'br', 'mx');
CREATE TABLE users_other  PARTITION OF users DEFAULT;  -- catch-all partition
```

## HASH Partitioning

```sql
CREATE TABLE audit_logs (
    id          BIGINT,
    user_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
    action      TEXT,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ
) PARTITION BY HASH (user_id);

-- 4 equal partitions
CREATE TABLE audit_logs_0 PARTITION OF audit_logs FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0);
CREATE TABLE audit_logs_1 PARTITION OF audit_logs FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 1);
CREATE TABLE audit_logs_2 PARTITION OF audit_logs FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 2);
CREATE TABLE audit_logs_3 PARTITION OF audit_logs FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 3);
```

## Sub-Partitioning

```sql
-- Partition by year, then hash within each year for even distribution
CREATE TABLE events_2024 PARTITION OF events
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2025-01-01')
    PARTITION BY HASH (user_id);

CREATE TABLE events_2024_h0 PARTITION OF events_2024
    FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0);
-- etc.
```

## Monitoring Partition Sizes

```sql
SELECT
    parent.relname AS parent_table,
    child.relname  AS partition,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(child.oid)) AS size,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(child.oid)) AS total_size
FROM pg_inherits
JOIN pg_class parent ON pg_inherits.inhparent = parent.oid
JOIN pg_class child  ON pg_inherits.inhrelid  = child.oid
WHERE parent.relname = 'orders'
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(child.oid) DESC;
```

questions.title: PostgreSQL Replication and High Availability
questions.question: How does PostgreSQL replication work and what high availability patterns are used with Spring Boot?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Streaming replication: primary sends WAL to standbys continuously
- Synchronous vs asynchronous: synchronous guarantees no data loss on failover; async is faster
- Read replicas: route read-only queries to standbys to scale reads
- Logical replication: replicate specific tables to other databases (different versions, different schemas)
- Failover: promote a standby to primary — requires reconfiguring application connection strings
- Spring: AbstractRoutingDataSource to route reads to replica, writes to primary
- Patroni / pg_auto_failover: automated failover orchestration

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
PostgreSQL replication works by having the primary server stream its write-ahead log to one or more standby servers. The standbys apply the WAL changes to their own data files, keeping them in sync. Standbys can serve read-only queries, which lets you scale read traffic horizontally by adding more replicas.

The consistency tradeoff is synchronous versus asynchronous replication. Asynchronous replication, the default, commits on the primary and sends WAL to the standby without waiting for confirmation. Reads on the standby might lag by a fraction of a second. If the primary fails before the standby receives the last WAL records, those writes are lost. Synchronous replication waits for at least one standby to confirm before the primary acknowledges the commit — no data loss, but higher write latency.

For a Spring Boot application, the standard pattern for using read replicas is a routing data source. You configure two data sources — one pointing to the primary for writes, one to a read replica — and use a TransactionSynchronizationManager or AbstractRoutingDataSource to route each transaction to the appropriate source based on whether it's read-only.

questions.title: Mastering EXPLAIN ANALYZE
questions.question: How do you read and interpret PostgreSQL EXPLAIN ANALYZE output to optimize queries?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Cost: planner's estimated cost in arbitrary units; actual time in ms is more useful
- Rows estimated vs actual: large difference = stale statistics, run ANALYZE
- Node types: Seq Scan (full table), Index Scan (b-tree lookup), Index Only Scan (no heap), Bitmap Heap Scan
- Hash Join, Merge Join, Nested Loop — know when each is appropriate
- Buffers: shared hit (from cache) vs read (from disk)
- Width: bytes per row — wide rows = more I/O per fetch
- Filter vs Index Cond: filter removes rows AFTER fetch, Index Cond uses index to avoid fetching

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The most important thing to look at in an EXPLAIN ANALYZE output is the difference between estimated rows and actual rows at each node. When the planner thinks a step will return 100 rows but it actually returns 50,000, the planner made bad decisions downstream based on that wrong estimate. This happens when table statistics are stale — running ANALYZE on the table refreshes the statistics.

The distinction between Filter and Index Cond in a scan node tells you a lot. Index Cond means the condition was pushed into the index scan — only matching rows are fetched. Filter means rows were fetched from the table and then discarded because they didn't match. A high "Rows Removed by Filter" count means the index isn't filtering enough or the wrong columns are indexed.

Buffers output with ANALYZE shows you how many pages came from the shared buffer cache versus disk. A high read count on a small table suggests it's being evicted from cache, possibly because shared_buffers is too small or queries are hitting many different tables.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Reading the Output

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE, FORMAT TEXT)
SELECT p.name, c.name AS category, p.price
FROM products p
JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.id
WHERE p.price > 100
ORDER BY p.price DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

```
Limit  (cost=4321.89..4321.94 rows=20 width=64)
       (actual time=45.231..45.238 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=1234 read=89
  ->  Sort  (cost=4321.89..4358.64 rows=14700 width=64)
            (actual time=45.228..45.231 rows=20 loops=1)
      Sort Key: p.price DESC
      Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 26kB
      ->  Hash Join  (cost=85.50..3890.25 rows=14700 width=64)
                     (actual time=2.109..41.876 rows=14823 loops=1)
          Hash Cond: (p.category_id = c.id)
          Buffers: shared hit=1187 read=89
          ->  Seq Scan on products p
              (cost=0..3250.00 rows=14700 width=56)
              (actual time=0.021..35.192 rows=14823 loops=1)
              Filter: (price > 100)
              Rows Removed by Filter: 45177  ← 45k rows scanned, 14k useful
              Buffers: shared hit=1150 read=89
          ->  Hash  (cost=55.00..55.00 rows=2440 width=20)
                    (actual time=1.876..1.876 rows=2440 loops=1)
              ->  Seq Scan on categories c
                  (cost=0..55.00 rows=2440 width=20)
```

**Analysis:**
- 45,177 rows removed by Filter → add `CREATE INDEX ON products (price) WHERE price > 0;`
- read=89 → some pages from disk, mostly cached (hit=1150)
- Estimated rows (14700) vs actual (14823) → good estimate, stats are fresh

## Scan Type Cheat Sheet

| Scan Type | When Used | Good Sign? |
|-----------|-----------|------------|
| Seq Scan | No usable index | No (on large tables) |
| Index Scan | Index found for filter/join | Yes |
| Index Only Scan | Covering index, no heap needed | Best |
| Bitmap Heap Scan | Multiple index conditions | Good for medium selectivity |

## Quick Wins Checklist

1. Seq Scan on table > 10k rows → add index
2. Rows Removed by Filter > 10x actual rows → better index or filter pushdown
3. Estimated vs actual rows differ by 10x+ → run ANALYZE
4. Nested Loop with large outer table + Seq Scan inner → index inner join column
5. Sort with large memory → consider pre-sorted index or ORDER BY with index

questions.question: What are window functions in PostgreSQL? Explain RANK, ROW_NUMBER, and LEAD/LAG with examples.
questions.title: PostgreSQL Window Functions — RANK, ROW_NUMBER, LAG/LEAD
questions.direct_answer: Window functions perform calculations across related rows without grouping them away. RANK/DENSE_RANK compute position within a partition. ROW_NUMBER assigns unique sequential numbers. LAG/LEAD access previous/next row values without a self-join.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can solve ranking and trend analysis problems without complex subqueries
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using RANK vs ROW_NUMBER incorrectly — RANK leaves gaps for ties, ROW_NUMBER never does
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER with tie examples and explain the OVER clause components

sections.content: Window functions are PostgreSQL's answer to the 'how do I compute per-row rankings or trend data without losing rows via GROUP BY?' question. The OVER clause defines the window: which rows participate (PARTITION BY) and in what order (ORDER BY).

-- Sample data:
-- employees: id, dept, name, salary

-- RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER (shows tie behavior)
SELECT
    name, dept, salary,
    RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_rank,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS row_num
FROM employees;

-- For two employees in ENG with salary=95000:
-- name     | dept | salary | rank | dense_rank | row_num
-- Alice    | ENG  | 95000  |  1   |     1      |   1
-- Bob      | ENG  | 95000  |  1   |     1      |   2  ← row_num always unique
-- Charlie  | ENG  | 80000  |  3   |     2      |   3  ← rank skips to 3, dense_rank=2

-- LAG/LEAD: access adjacent rows (no self-join needed)
SELECT
    month,
    revenue,
    LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month)  AS prev_month_revenue,
    LEAD(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS next_month_revenue,
    revenue - LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS month_over_month_delta
FROM monthly_sales
ORDER BY month;

-- Find top-1 earner per department (use ROW_NUMBER for unique top-1)
SELECT name, dept, salary
FROM (
    SELECT name, dept, salary,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn
    FROM employees
) t
WHERE rn = 1;

- **ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK on ties** — `RANK` skips numbers after ties (1,1,3); `DENSE_RANK` does not (1,1,2); `ROW_NUMBER` assigns arbitrary unique integers; choose based on whether gaps in ranking matter to the use case
- **ROW_NUMBER deduplication** — `PARTITION BY entity_id ORDER BY created_at DESC` + outer `WHERE rn = 1` keeps the latest row per group; replaces correlated subqueries and self-joins
- **Window functions run after WHERE and GROUP BY** — cannot filter on window results in WHERE; wrap in a CTE or subquery, then apply the filter in the outer query
- **LAG/LEAD eliminate self-joins for row comparison** — `amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month)` computes period-over-period change in one pass; a self-join on date equality does the same with more complexity
- **PARTITION BY is optional** — omitting it applies the function globally across all rows; adding it scopes the calculation to each partition independently

Window functions perform calculations across related rows without collapsing them — unlike GROUP BY which gives you one row per group, window functions annotate every row with a computed value while keeping all rows visible.

**ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK — the tie question**
- `ROW_NUMBER()` assigns unique sequential integers regardless of ties — so two employees with the same salary get 1 and 2 arbitrarily
- `RANK()` assigns the same number to ties but skips after them (1, 1, 3) — so the next-highest salary is rank 3, not rank 2
- `DENSE_RANK()` assigns the same number to ties and doesn't skip (1, 1, 2) — which means the next-highest salary is always one step above the tied group; use this when gaps in ranking would be confusing to users

**PARTITION BY and ORDER BY — the two control levers**
- `PARTITION BY` divides rows into groups for the window function to operate within — `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC)` ranks each employee within their department, not globally
- Without PARTITION BY, the function operates across the entire result set; combining both gives you group-scoped rankings without GROUP BY

**Deduplication with ROW_NUMBER**
- The most common production use: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)` assigns rank 1 to each user's latest record — wrap it in a CTE or subquery and filter `WHERE rn = 1` to keep only the latest row per user without a correlated subquery or self-join

**LAG and LEAD for row-to-row comparisons**
- `LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month)` returns the previous row's value — `amount - LAG(amount)` computes month-over-month change in one pass, eliminating a self-join on date columns
- `SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)` computes a running total without any subquery

Window functions execute after WHERE and GROUP BY but before ORDER BY — filter on window function results by wrapping the query in a CTE or subquery.

questions.question: What types of indexes does PostgreSQL support? When do you use each?
questions.title: PostgreSQL Index Types — B-Tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, Hash
questions.direct_answer: B-Tree is the default for equality and range queries. GIN is for full-text search and JSONB queries. GiST handles geometric and range types. BRIN is extremely compact for naturally ordered large tables. Hash is fast for equality only.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know more than just 'add an index' — correct index type for the access pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using B-Tree for JSONB attribute queries (requires GIN) or for full-text search
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain partial indexes, covering indexes (INCLUDE), and when to use expression indexes

sections.content: Index type selection is about matching the index data structure to the access pattern. B-Tree's sorted structure handles range queries perfectly. GIN's inverted index handles multi-value containment efficiently. Wrong index type = index that exists but is never used.

| Index Type | Best For | Operators Supported | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| B-Tree (default) | Equality, ranges, ORDER BY | =, <, >, <=, >=, BETWEEN | Covers 90% of use cases |
| GIN | JSONB, arrays, full-text search | @>, <@, @@, @@ | Large index size, slow writes |
| GiST | Geometry, ranges, nearest-neighbor | &&, <<, >>, @> | Used by PostGIS |
| BRIN | Very large tables, sequential data | =, < ,> (approx) | Tiny size, great for time series |
| Hash | Equality only, no ranges | = | Rarely better than B-Tree |

**Practical examples:**
```sql
-- B-Tree (default): user lookups, date ranges
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created
    ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);

-- GIN: JSONB attribute queries
CREATE INDEX idx_products_attrs
    ON products USING GIN (attributes);
-- Enables: WHERE attributes @> '{"color": "red"}'

-- GIN: Full-text search
CREATE INDEX idx_articles_search
    ON articles USING GIN (to_tsvector('english', title || ' ' || body));
-- Enables: WHERE to_tsvector(...) @@ to_tsquery('postgresql')

-- BRIN: IoT sensor data (ordered by time)
CREATE INDEX idx_sensor_time
    ON sensor_readings USING BRIN (recorded_at);
-- 1000x smaller than B-Tree, perfect for time series

-- Partial index: only active users
CREATE INDEX idx_active_users_email
    ON users (email)
    WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';

-- Covering index (INCLUDE): eliminates heap fetch
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_covering
    ON orders (user_id)
    INCLUDE (status, total_amount, created_at);
-- Query: SELECT status, total_amount FROM orders WHERE user_id=42
-- → Index Only Scan (never touches the table!)

-- Expression index: case-insensitive lookup
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower
    ON users (LOWER(email));
-- WHERE LOWER(email) = 'user@example.com'
```

- **GIN for JSONB containment and full-text search** — `@>` (contains) and `@@` (text search) operators use GIN; B-tree cannot index multi-value or inverted lookup patterns
- **GiST for geometric and range types** — overlap, containment, and nearest-neighbor queries on geometry and range columns; the only index type that handles spatial operators
- **Composite B-tree left-prefix rule** — `(a, b)` cannot serve `WHERE b = ?` alone; the leading column must be in the filter
- **Partial index reduces index size and maintenance cost** — `WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'` indexes only active rows; as completed records accumulate, the index doesn't grow; aligned precisely with the queries that matter
- **Expression index enables computed predicates** — `CREATE INDEX ON users(LOWER(email))` is required for `WHERE LOWER(email) = ?`; a plain `email` index cannot satisfy a case-insensitive lookup

PostgreSQL's index type selection starts with B-tree — it handles equality, ranges, and ORDER BY for the vast majority of queries. GIN and GiST exist for the cases B-tree can't handle: multi-value types and geometric data.

**B-tree — sorted, versatile, the default**
- B-tree keeps values in sorted order, which means it handles `=`, `>`, `<`, `BETWEEN`, `LIKE 'prefix%'`, and `ORDER BY` all from one structure; it's the index you get with `CREATE INDEX` without specifying a type
- Composite B-tree indexes follow the left-prefix rule — an index on `(user_id, status)` serves `WHERE user_id = ?` or both columns, but not `WHERE status = ?` alone

**GIN — for multi-value types**
- GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes every element inside a composite value — which means `WHERE data @> '{"role": "admin"}'` on a JSONB column uses a GIN index to find documents containing that key-value pair without scanning every row
- GIN also powers full-text search: `CREATE INDEX ON articles USING GIN(to_tsvector('english', body))` lets `WHERE body_search @@ to_tsquery('spring & boot')` use an index
- GIN is built once and is slower to update than B-tree, but extremely fast for containment queries on arrays, JSONB, and tsvector

**GiST — for geometric and range types**
- GiST (Generalized Search Tree) supports overlap, containment, and nearest-neighbor queries on geometric data types and range types
- `CREATE INDEX ON locations USING GIST(coordinates)` supports `WHERE coordinates && BOX(...)` — finding all points within a bounding box — which B-tree can't express

**Partial and expression indexes**
- A partial index with a WHERE clause indexes only matching rows: `CREATE INDEX ON orders(user_id) WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'` — smaller, faster to maintain, precisely aligned with the query
- An expression index on `LOWER(email)` enables case-insensitive equality lookups without a full scan

questions.question: What are PostgreSQL transaction isolation levels? Explain the anomalies they prevent.
questions.title: PostgreSQL Transaction Isolation Levels
questions.direct_answer: PostgreSQL supports Read Committed (default), Repeatable Read, and Serializable. Each prevents different concurrency anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads. PostgreSQL implements these via MVCC — readers never block writers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of MVCC and why Read Committed is safe for most queries
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Serializable for all transactions — it has significant overhead and retry logic is required
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) as PostgreSQL's mechanism for isolation, and why readers never block

sections.content: Concurrency anomalies occur when multiple transactions run simultaneously. Higher isolation prevents more anomalies but reduces concurrency. PostgreSQL's MVCC means reads always see a consistent snapshot — no reader blocks a writer, no writer blocks a reader.

| Level | Dirty Read | Non-Repeatable Read | Phantom Read | Serialization Anomaly |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Read Committed (default) | ✅ Prevented | ❌ Possible | ❌ Possible | ❌ Possible |
| Repeatable Read | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented* | ❌ Possible |
| Serializable | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented |

*PostgreSQL Repeatable Read also prevents phantom reads (exceeds SQL standard requirement)

**Anomaly definitions:**
- **Dirty Read**: Read uncommitted data from another transaction (would roll back)
- **Non-Repeatable Read**: Re-reading a row gives different result (another transaction committed)
- **Phantom Read**: Re-running a query finds new rows (another transaction inserted)
- **Serialization Anomaly**: Result only possible if transactions didn't run concurrently

- **PostgreSQL MVCC: readers never block writers** — each row version is visible to the transactions that should see it; reads take a snapshot instead of acquiring shared locks
- **Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL also prevents phantom reads** — the MVCC snapshot taken at transaction start excludes rows inserted after; MySQL Repeatable Read requires gap locks and still has edge cases
- **Serializable uses SSI, not lock-based** — PostgreSQL detects dangerous read-write dependency cycles and aborts one transaction; lower contention than traditional lock-based Serializable isolation
- **Write skew requires Serializable** — two transactions each read shared state, make valid changes, and both commit — producing a state no serial execution could reach; only Serializable prevents this
- **Long transactions cause VACUUM bloat** — MVCC keeps old row versions alive while any transaction might need them; a long-running transaction blocks VACUUM from reclaiming dead rows, causing table bloat

PostgreSQL implements isolation levels through MVCC — Multi-Version Concurrency Control. Every row has a version; when a transaction reads a row that another transaction is modifying, it sees the older version rather than blocking. This is why readers never block writers in PostgreSQL.

**Read Committed — the PostgreSQL default**
- Each statement in a transaction sees a fresh snapshot of committed data — which means two reads of the same row within one transaction may return different values if another transaction commits between them (non-repeatable read)
- This is the right default for most OLTP workloads and eliminates the need for shared locks on reads; most applications run correctly under Read Committed

**Repeatable Read — consistent snapshot from transaction start**
- PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read takes a snapshot at transaction start and holds it for all reads — which means the same row always returns the same value within one transaction, even if other transactions commit changes in between
- Unlike MySQL, PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read also prevents phantom reads via MVCC — no gap locks needed because the snapshot simply doesn't show rows inserted after the snapshot was taken

**Serializable — prevents write skew**
- Serializable is the only level that prevents write skew — the anomaly where two transactions read overlapping data, make independent decisions, and both commit, leaving the database in a state no serial execution could produce
- PostgreSQL implements Serializable using Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) — it detects dangerous read-write dependencies and aborts one transaction rather than using traditional pessimistic locks; lower contention than lock-based Serializable

**MVCC trade-off: table bloat**
- Old row versions are kept until no active transaction needs them — which means long-running transactions prevent VACUUM from reclaiming space, causing table and index bloat; this is the most common PostgreSQL operational problem related to isolation

questions.question: How do you work with JSONB in PostgreSQL? When should you use JSONB vs relational columns?
questions.title: PostgreSQL JSONB — Queries, Indexing, and When to Use It
questions.direct_answer: JSONB stores JSON as binary for fast querying and indexing. Use JSONB for semi-structured or schema-flexible attributes (product metadata, user preferences). Use relational columns for data you filter, join, or aggregate frequently — indexes on JSONB are less efficient than on typed columns.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical JSONB query knowledge and understanding of trade-offs vs relational design
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using JSONB for everything ('document database in PostgreSQL') — loses all relational benefits
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the @> containment operator and jsonb_each() for iterating keys, and when GIN vs B-Tree indexes apply

sections.content: JSONB stores JSON in a binary decomposed format — keys are sorted, types are preserved, and duplicate keys are removed. It supports operators for containment, key existence, and path traversal. GIN indexes make JSONB queries fast.

-- JSONB column definition:
CREATE TABLE products (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,
    price       NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,   -- typed column for aggregation
    category    TEXT NOT NULL,             -- typed for joins
    attributes  JSONB                      -- semi-structured metadata
);

-- Sample data:
INSERT INTO products VALUES
(1, 'Widget Pro', 29.99, 'electronics',
 '{"color": "red", "weight_kg": 0.5, "tags": ["sale", "new"]}');

-- JSONB OPERATORS:
-- -> returns JSON:  attributes -> 'color' → '"red"'
-- ->> returns text: attributes ->> 'color' → 'red'
-- @> containment:   attributes @> '{"color": "red"}'
-- ? key exists:     attributes ? 'weight_kg'
-- #> path:          attributes #> '{specs,cpu}'

-- Query by JSONB attribute:
SELECT name, attributes ->> 'color' AS color
FROM products
WHERE attributes @> '{"color": "red"}'   -- uses GIN index!
  AND attributes ? 'weight_kg';           -- key exists

-- Expand JSONB to rows:
SELECT name, key, value
FROM products,
     jsonb_each_text(attributes) AS kv(key, value)
WHERE category = 'electronics';

-- Update a specific JSONB key:
UPDATE products
SET attributes = jsonb_set(attributes, '{color}', '"blue"')
WHERE id = 1;

-- GIN index for containment queries:
CREATE INDEX idx_products_attrs_gin
    ON products USING GIN (attributes);
-- Now @> and ? operators use the index

sections.title: JSONB Query Patterns and Indexing Strategies
sections.content:
JSONB's power comes from its operator-based query language and GIN indexing. Knowing which operators are index-supported prevents full-table scans on JSONB columns.

**Containment operator (@>) for equality queries.** The `@>` operator checks if the left JSONB value contains the right value. This is the most GIN-index-friendly operator: `WHERE metadata @> '{"status": "active"}'` uses a GIN index efficiently. Use it instead of `->>`  comparison when checking for exact key-value matches.

**Path operators for nested access.** Use `->` to access a JSON object key and get a JSONB result. Use `->>` to get a text result. Use `#>` and `#>>` for nested path access: `metadata #>> '{address,city}'` extracts a deeply nested value. For WHERE clauses, prefer `@>` containment when possible because it uses GIN indexes; `->>`  text extraction requires a separate expression index.

```sql
-- GIN index covers containment queries
CREATE INDEX idx_products_metadata ON products USING GIN (metadata);

-- Efficient: uses GIN index
SELECT * FROM products WHERE metadata @> '{"brand": "Acme"}';

-- Inefficient: GIN index does NOT cover ->> extraction
SELECT * FROM products WHERE metadata ->> 'brand' = 'Acme';

-- Fix: create an expression index for ->> queries
CREATE INDEX idx_products_brand ON products ((metadata ->> 'brand'));
```

**When to extract JSONB fields into relational columns.** If you query or aggregate on a JSONB field frequently (e.g., filtering products by `metadata->>'brand'` in every listing page), extract it into a proper relational column with a regular B-tree index. JSONB is ideal for semi-structured data that varies between rows (custom attributes, user preferences, integration payloads). It is a poor choice for data you filter, sort, or join on regularly — relational columns with proper types and indexes outperform JSONB for these access patterns.

**JSONB in Spring Data JPA.** Use Hibernate's `@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON)` annotation (Hibernate 6+) to map a Java object to a JSONB column. Spring Data's `@Query` with `nativeQuery = true` is required for JSONB operators because JPQL has no JSONB support. Alternatively, use the Specification pattern with a native SQL fragment for dynamic JSONB filters.

- **`jsonb` over `json` always** — `json` re-parses text on every read; `jsonb` stores binary, supports GIN indexing, and returns field extractions fast
- **GIN index enables `@>` containment queries** — `CREATE INDEX ... USING GIN(data)` lets `WHERE data @> '{"status": "active"}'` avoid a full table scan
- **Expression index for specific-key equality** — `CREATE INDEX ON t ((data->>'email'))` enables `WHERE data->>'email' = ?` to use an index; a plain GIN index won't help equality on one extracted field
- **`->>` returns text; `->` returns JSON** — chain `->` for nested navigation, use `->>` at the final step for text comparison in WHERE; `WHERE data->>'count' = '5'` (text) not `= 5` (integer) unless you cast
- **Use JSONB for sparse or schema-flexible attributes** — product metadata, feature flags, and multi-tenant configuration benefit from JSONB; core relational attributes that appear on every row belong in typed columns with B-tree indexes

PostgreSQL's JSONB type stores JSON as binary and supports rich query operations with GIN indexing — making it possible to query semi-structured data at near-relational speed without leaving the relational database.

**JSONB vs JSON**
- `json` stores the raw text verbatim and re-parses it on every access — which means querying `json` columns is slower because the parsing happens each time
- `jsonb` stores JSON as parsed binary, which means field lookups are fast and the column can be GIN-indexed; this is the right choice for any JSON column you'll query

**Key operators**
- `->>` extracts a field as text: `data->>'status'` returns the status value as a string — used in WHERE clauses for equality filters
- `->` extracts a field as a JSON value: `data->'address'->>'city'` drills into nested objects
- `@>` checks containment: `WHERE data @> '{"role": "admin"}'` — returns documents where the JSON contains that key-value pair; this is the operator that uses a GIN index

**GIN indexing for fast containment queries**
- `CREATE INDEX ON users USING GIN(data)` — GIN indexes every key-value pair in the JSONB column, which means `WHERE data @> '{"role": "admin"}'` uses the index instead of scanning every row
- For equality on a specific key: `CREATE INDEX ON users ((data->>'email'))` — an expression index on the extracted field, used by `WHERE data->>'email' = ?`

**When to use JSONB vs normalized columns**
- Use JSONB for schema-flexible or sparse attributes — product metadata, feature flags, user preferences where different records legitimately have different fields
- Use normalized columns for core, always-present attributes that you filter, sort, or join on frequently — those benefit from typed columns with direct B-tree indexes

questions.question: Why do you need connection pooling for PostgreSQL? Compare PgBouncer modes.
questions.title: PostgreSQL Connection Pooling with PgBouncer
questions.direct_answer: PostgreSQL forks a process per connection — thousands of connections exhaust memory and hurt performance. PgBouncer pools connections, routing application connections to a smaller set of PostgreSQL server connections. Transaction mode is optimal for most Spring Boot applications.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of PostgreSQL's connection cost model and pooling trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Session mode in PgBouncer with connection limits — same as no pooling for high-concurrency apps
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the HikariCP (application-side) + PgBouncer (server-side) two-tier pooling pattern and why both are needed at scale

sections.content: PostgreSQL spawns a backend process per connection (not a thread). Each process uses ~5MB RAM. 1000 connections = 5GB just for idle connection overhead. PgBouncer sits between application and PostgreSQL, multiplexing many application connections to few server connections.

-- PostgreSQL connection cost:
-- SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity; → see current connections
-- SHOW max_connections; → default 100 (too low for microservices!)

-- Without pooling: 10 microservice instances × 10 HikariCP connections = 100 connections
-- Add Kubernetes scaling to 50 instances: 500 connections → PostgreSQL refuses!

-- PgBouncer pooling modes:
-- 1. SESSION mode: one server connection per client session
--    Client connects → gets dedicated PG connection for entire session
--    No benefit for stateless HTTP services!

-- 2. TRANSACTION mode (recommended for Spring Boot):
--    Client gets a PG connection only during a transaction
--    100 app connections, only 20 PG connections needed (80% idle time)

-- 3. STATEMENT mode:
--    Connection released after each statement
--    CANNOT use transactions, prepared statements
--    Rarely used

-- PgBouncer config:
-- pgbouncer.ini:
-- [databases]
-- mydb = host=postgres port=5432 dbname=mydb
-- [pgbouncer]
-- pool_mode = transaction          ← CRITICAL SETTING
-- max_client_conn = 1000           ← app connections
-- default_pool_size = 20           ← pg connections per database
-- server_pool_size = 5             ← max additional server connections

// Spring Boot datasource pointing to PgBouncer:
// spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://pgbouncer:6432/mydb
// spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=50  ← connects to PgBouncer
// PgBouncer maps these 50 to 20 PG server connections

- **PostgreSQL forks a process per connection** — not a thread; 500 connections = 500 OS processes; each idle connection consumes ~5-10MB RAM plus a backend process slot
- **PgBouncer transaction pooling: many clients, few PostgreSQL connections** — a single PostgreSQL connection handles many application requests serially; 10 real connections can serve 1,000 concurrent clients without 1,000 PostgreSQL processes
- **Transaction pooling vs session pooling** — transaction mode is most efficient (connection held only during the transaction); session mode holds it for the client session; statement mode is incompatible with multi-statement transactions
- **Prepared statements require configuration with PgBouncer** — transaction pooling mode breaks server-side prepared statements; set `prepareThreshold=0` in HikariCP or use `DISCARD ALL` after each connection return
- **HikariCP + PgBouncer as two layers** — HikariCP manages app-to-PgBouncer connections; PgBouncer manages PgBouncer-to-PostgreSQL connections; monitor both pool wait times independently

PostgreSQL creates a separate OS process per connection — not a thread, a full process. That means each idle connection consumes memory and a backend process slot even when it's doing nothing, which is the fundamental reason connection pooling is mandatory at scale.

**Why PostgreSQL needs external pooling**
- At 500 concurrent connections, PostgreSQL is running 500 backend processes — each consuming roughly 5-10MB of RAM just for the process overhead, before any query is executed
- Most web applications open far more connections than they need — a Spring Boot app with 50 threads per instance and 10 instances creates 500 connections at startup, most of them idle
- PgBouncer sits between the application and PostgreSQL, maintaining a small pool of real PostgreSQL connections while accepting many more from the application side

**PgBouncer pooling modes**
- Transaction pooling is the most efficient — the PostgreSQL connection is only held for the duration of a transaction, then returned to the pool; a single PostgreSQL connection can serve many application requests serially, which means 10 PostgreSQL connections can serve 1,000 concurrent application connections
- Session pooling holds the connection for the full client session — semantically identical to a direct connection; useful for compatibility but provides less multiplexing benefit
- Statement pooling holds the connection for a single statement — most efficient but incompatible with transactions and prepared statements; rarely used

**HikariCP + PgBouncer together**
- HikariCP manages the application-side connection pool to PgBouncer; PgBouncer manages the PostgreSQL-side pool — the two layers reduce connection count at both the application and database levels
- With transaction pooling, disable prepared statements at the PgBouncer level or configure HikariCP to use simple statements: `spring.datasource.hikari.data-source-properties.prepareThreshold=0`
